lines.note: The Japanese describes sparrows gathered together; the Portuguese begins 'a flock of sparrows'. The scan reads par-, not the draft's per-, and the word continues in the next physical row.

Completes pardaes and introduces an example about sparrows coming together competitively to form a market-like gathering. The Japanese example continues below; its roman type is distinct from italic Vt.
Completes the Japanese example with naſu and begins its Portuguese explanation: many sparrows gathering make a commotion. Keep the printed Ajuntandoſe and pardaes rather than modernizing them.
Completes the preceding gloss with bustle and noise. This is a continuation of the sparrow example, not a separate entry.
A separate homonymous entry names a small bird. The definition does not identify its species, so the transcription and note do not expand it beyond what the scan supplies.

Names a horse-coat colour, described as grey with star-like markings. The entry continues with a second colour description on the next row; preserve the printed headword rather than regularizing it to a modern spelling.
Completes the horse-colour gloss with dappled grey. The initial ou links it directly to the previous line.
The entry denotes a kind of lattice or grating. The nasal abbreviation in Hũa is visible and is retained, with Portuguese in italic.
Fiuo tçuranuru explains successive days, matching the Portuguese 'continuous days'. The terminal t in Renjit is a historical headword spelling, not a missing modern suffix to supply.
The pilcrow introduces a Japanese example of conversing or exchanging communications over successive days. The Portuguese translation begins here and continues across two further rows.
Continues the translation: over many successive days we converse and communicate. The printed commu- has a line-end hyphen and joins nicamos below.
Completes communicamos from the preceding row. No new entry or sentence beginning is introduced here.
A homonym of the 'successive days' entry: Faſuno mi identifies lotus fruit, rendered with the Portuguese plant name golfão. The word-final nasal mark falls over the a in golfão on this row.
Defines a letter signed by many people. The headword has no visible length accent here, unlike the variant explicitly supplied on the following row.
Gives the accented variant of the preceding jointly signed letter. The open, downward-pointing accent is retained as ǒ; Idem refers to the previous entry rather than an independent definition.
Nerimigaqu describes practising and polishing one's ability. The Portuguese po- continues as lirſe on the next row, with the printed line-end hyphen preserved.
Completes polirſe and introduces an example about skill acquired through practice. The circumflex in cô is visible, and mui- continues below as to.
Completes 'much practice' in the preceding example's gloss. The line is entirely Portuguese italic, including its closing punctuation.
Defines the continuous progression of something without interruption. The tilde in dalgũa is retained in its printed position.
Completes the uninterrupted-continuation definition. This short indented row belongs to Renmen above.
Auaremi matches mercy or compassion; the Portuguese pairs miſericordia with piedade. The latter is physically divided as pie-/dade.
Completes piedade and supplies verbal constructions for showing mercy. The alternative marker and Japanese expressions are roman, not part of the italic Portuguese gloss.
Translates both preceding verbal constructions as exercising compassion and mercy. Preserve initial V in Vſar and the printed historical spelling.
Again identifies lotus fruit, now with medicinal use specified below. The scan ends in ſer without a visible hyphen; do not add one merely because ſerue is split across rows.
Completes ſerue and states that the lotus fruit serves as medicine. The historical form mezinha is retained, not replaced with a modern medical term.

Xiroi faſu gives white lotus flowers. The Portuguese initial is G, not the draft's C; the separate final S. is a roman register label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
The Japanese gloss relates to succession or continuity, while the Portuguese begins 'many times, or'. The comma and inflectional u remain part of the Japanese explanation.
Completes the adverbial definition and begins an example about repeatedly saying something. Renren is divided physically as ren-/ren, with the printed hyphen retained.
Completes the Japanese repeated-action example and its Portuguese translation, 'I said this on several occasions'. The pilcrow and abbreviated Itẽ introduce an additional sense below.
Gives the additional sense 'little by little'. It belongs to Renren and is not a new headword.

Introduces a branch joined or intertwined with another. The e immediately after R in the example Renrino is abraded; the surviving letters and preceding headword support the retained reading, but the damaged glyph is not fully legible.
Completes the joined-branch image and introduces another use. Preserve the printed emburulhado rather than silently regularizing its spelling.
The abbreviated permet. introduces a metaphorical application: deep friendship and union. The following Japanese example belongs to this figurative sense, not the literal branch description.
The Japanese example describes making a closely joined bond; the Portuguese begins 'to have friendship'. The continuation qualifies the closeness of that relationship.

runs.text: muito eſtreita, como a de dous caſados, &c.

lines.note: Completes the example with friendship as close as that of two married people. The historical dous and eſtreita are retained, with no modernization of the comparison.
Yedauo tçuranuru describes connected branches. The Portuguese nasal mark in eſtaõ is printed over the o and is kept there; the metaphorical extension continues below.

runs.text: pegados, & continuados na aruore: mas toma

lines.note: Continues the literal description of branches connected in a tree, then signals a usual transferred meaning. The scan divides toma/ſe without a visible hyphen, which is not supplied.
States that the expression is commonly used for siblings and begins a Japanese example. The printed comummente is retained; the pilcrow separates the gloss from the example.
Completes Renxino chiguiri and translates it as the union and friendship of siblings. The close setting of &amizade is retained as in the scan.
Auaremu cocoro denotes a compassionate heart, matching Coração piadoſo. This is a separate entry, not the completion of the sibling example.
Youo tçuranuru explains successive nights. The Portuguese adjective is divided as continua-/das, and the hyphen at the right edge is visible.
Completes the successive-nights definition. The final S. is a separate roman label rather than part of the italic adjective. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Fachiſuno fa identifies lotus leaves. The headword begins with R, not the draft's B; its circumflex is visible. Retain the final-o tilde in golfaõ and the separate roman S. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Gives Reô and Riô as alternatives and Tatçu as the Japanese gloss, translated here as Lagarto. The historical Portuguese wording is retained, although the Japanese denotes a dragon; both circumflexes and the printed punctuation are preserved.
Feya identifies a room or chamber. The accent and upper part of the final vowel are worn; retain the aligned ǒ rather than imposing the circumflex from neighbouring, different headwords.

Defines hunting or fishing and begins a verbal example. At the right edge the small letter between R and ô is almost entirely abraded; Riô- is retained from the aligned reading and the preceding alternative, with that uncertainty explicit.

Completes Riôuo ſuru as 'to hunt or fish' and begins a second example continued in column 2. The damaged middle letter of Reôga retains the lower curve of e, not a; the length mark is faint, so the restored reading remains a qualified one.

runs.text: Tomar algũa couſa na caça, ou peſcaria.

lines.note: Completes Reôga qiqu from the foot of column 1. The gloss concerns taking or catching something in hunting or fishing, not the ordinary modern sense of qiqu in isolation.

Mimixij and voxi are glossed as deaf and mute. Retain the conspicuous printed gap before a in the headword; the final S. is roman, and no absent full stop is inserted before it. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Norimono identifies a conveyance; the Portuguese specifies a royal litter. Remove the draft's spurious gap inside Reôca, but retain the printed alternative forms and punctuation rather than regularizing the i. marker.
Tabino marebito identifies a travelling guest, matching Hoſpede. There is no clearly printed length accent in the headword to add.

Satori xiru concerns understanding or insight. The Portuguese starts a definition in terms of reasoning or conjecture; enlargement confirms the short end mark after entendi-, so the printed division is preserved.
Completes entendimento and supplies conjecture as an alternative. The historical spelling conjeitura is legible and retained.
A distinct unaccented headword is glossed with knowing through consideration or assessment. The Portuguese gives knowledge or prudence, divided as pru-/dencia.
Completes prudencia from the preceding row. The full stop closes that entry before Reôco begins below.

Pairs the Japanese terms for dragon and tiger, using the source's Portuguese Lagarto for the former. Keep the circumflex and the historical translation rather than replacing it with modern zoological wording.
Defines two tigers and begins an illustrative comparison involving two tigers and two dragons. Both carons in Reǒco and the circumflex in nireôno are visible and distinguish the printed forms.
Completes the Japanese example as making a fight. Its Portuguese explanation begins with fighting or contending; contenderẽ has a visible final nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: duas peßoas prĩcipaes como dous tigres, ou dous

lines.note: Explains a struggle between two prominent people as that of two tigers or dragons. Restore the visible tilde in prĩcipaes and read the terminal word as dous, not the draft's dour; the comparison continues below.
Completes the dragon comparison using the dictionary's Portuguese lagartos. The penultimate consonant is t, not the draft's i; its cross-stroke is visible in the crop.
Defines reasoning thoroughly or discerning well. The a in taſſuru is worn, but the surrounding letters and Japanese construction support the retained aligned reading.

Completes the intellectual-reasoning definition and adds speculation as an alternative. Keep the final S. as a separate roman label, not inside the italic definition. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Names the lord or owner of revenue or land. Both headword alternatives carry carons, and the nasal abbreviations in dalgũa and rẽda remain unexpanded.
Completes the possession gloss by adding lands as an alternative to revenue. The short row belongs to Reǒju/Riǒju above.

runs.text: Figura de lagarto pintada, ou feita

lines.note: Defines a painted or embroidered dragon design using the source's word lagarto. The scan has feita, with an f cross-stroke, not the draft's ſeita.
Completes the description with embroidery or frame-work embroidery. Preserve the historical broslado and baſtidor instead of modernizing their spellings.
Reǒno vchi describes the inside of a chamber. The carons in both forms are visible and agree with the room sense, not the neighbouring dragon terms with circumflexes.

runs.text: Dentro das terras, ou territorio dalgũ

lines.note: A separate entry describes being within someone's lands or territory. The nasal mark over the last u abbreviates the final consonant of dalgũ.
Completes 'within the lands or territory of a lord'. This row is the continuation of the preceding territorial entry.

Defines a renowned horse and then a horse ridden by the king. Restore afamado from the draft's aſamado; its f is visible. Enlargement shows a small wave-shaped nasal mark in võ, not a caron. The supplied lexical index corroborates this reading but does not replace the scan: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

runs.text: lo em que caualga o Rey.

lines.note: Completes caualo and the alternative definition as a horse on which the king rides. Retain the printed Rey and the unmodernized verb spelling.
Facari, u relates to considering or devising a means; the Portuguese gives a remedy or expedient. The example begins at the right edge and is visibly divided Reô-/qenuo.
Completes the example meaning to provide a remedy. Retain the tight setting oureme- and the printed end mark, rather than adding an unprinted word space.
Completes remediar and starts the contrasting example with no remedy available. The nasal mark is over the o in Naõ, as printed.
Completes the negative gloss begun with Naõ. The infinitive auer retains the source's spelling and closes the Reôqen entry.
Mimixij is glossed as deaf. The example begins with judging right and wrong and is divided qi-/cazaru; retain the visible hyphen and the roman Japanese text.

Completes the comparison of failing to hear or distinguish right and wrong with deafness. The vowel after cot is damaged and open on its right; retain the aligned coteua rather than silently emending it to the expected cotoua. The chosen reading is uncertain.

runs.text: ouuir, & descernir o bem, & mal he como

lines.note: Continues the Portuguese explanation: not hearing and discerning good and evil is like being deaf. The spelling descernir is historical and remains as printed.
Completes the comparison with being deaf. The row is wholly Portuguese italic and does not begin a new entry.
Aya and vſumono identify fine patterned or light fabrics. The gloss begins with rich pieces of cloth or garments; veſti- continues below.
Completes the definition as garments of fine, thin silk and begins a Japanese example. The word qin is continued as xuuo on the next physical row without an added hyphen.
Completes the example about wearing fine silk or brocade. The circumflex in matô is legible; its Portuguese translation continues onto the short final row.
Completes the description as rich and fine pieces of cloth. A real space separates e from finas, correcting the draft's joined efinas.

Midare, ruru describes things mingled or in profusion. The headword begins R, not B, and the Portuguese reads Miſtura rather than the draft's Mißtura; the precise st/ſt ligature classification remains subject to the project's dedicated allograph review.

runs.text: muitas flores ou roſas que eſtaõ muito juntas,

lines.note: Continues the image of many flowers or roses close together. Preserve the nasal mark over the final o in eſtaõ and the comma at the right edge.

Completes the description as clustered or accumulated together. The final S. is a separate roman register label within the entry, not part of the italic adjective. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Defines prepared or seasoned food and supplies a verbal form for preparing it. Both headword and Japanese example are roman; Vt and the Portuguese gloss are italic.
Translates Reôri ſuru as preparing or seasoning food. It is the completion of the example, not another headword.

runs.text: Zombaria que ſe faz dalguem por

lines.note: Begins a definition of mockery or abusive treatment carried out against someone. The Portuguese sentence continues into the following row.
Specifies mistreatment by actions and completes the preceding definition. Preserve the printed maltratandoo, without inserting a modern clitic hyphen.
Defines the person who prepares or seasons food, that is, the cook. The circumflex in Reôrixa is visible and agrees with the preceding culinary entry.

Vomonbacari vomô concerns conceiving or considering something mentally; the gloss begins 'image, or'. Keep the caron in Reoſǒ distinct from the circumflex in vomô; the final Portuguese ou is faint but present.

runs.text: eſpecie de couſa q̃ hũ tem viua na imaginação.

lines.note: Completes the definition as an image of something held vividly in the imagination. Both q̃ and hũ retain their nasal abbreviation marks; the scan also shows a closing full stop missing from the draft.

Tabino ſô identifies a travelling religious person. Restore the clearly printed Reoſô, not the draft's Beuio, and Religioſo eſtrãgeiro in place of the garbled Portuguese; the circumflexes and the tilde in eſtrãgeiro are visible. There is no visible full stop after the final roman S, and none is supplied.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: Bottom-right catchword, separate from the last dictionary entry; the middle e is partly abraded.
